item.title: 11 days not enough for Fijians to understand proposed Constitution changes – Vuki
item.description: Ordinary Fijians cannot be expected to understand complex constitutional changes in just 11 days, and need more time to make informed submissions on proposals that could shape the country's future. This is the concern raised by Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission Commissioner Alefia Vuki, who says people need proper public education, clear explanations and sufficient time to under
item.content:encoded:
Ordinary Fijians cannot be expected to understand complex constitutional changes in just 11 days, and need more time to make informed submissions on proposals that could shape the country's future.

This is the concern raised by Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission Commissioner Alefia Vuki, who says people need proper public education, clear explanations and sufficient time to understand the proposed amendments.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Vuki says the Constitution is a complex legal document, and people should not be expected to fully understand the proposed changes within such a short period.

She says the Government should provide public education on the 2013 Constitution, the Constitutional Review Commission's report, the proposed amendments and the Government's revised draft.

Vuki says people also need time to seek advice from teachers, doctors and others in their communities who can help explain the proposals.

She is calling for the documents to be translated into iTaukei and Hindi, while the English versions should be written in plain language to make them easier to understand.

Vuki stresses that people cannot make informed decisions if they do not understand what is being proposed.

She says the Commission supports amending the 2013 Constitution because it believes the document was imposed on the people.

However, Vuki says the Commission's main concern is not whether the Constitution should be changed, but how the changes are being carried out.

She says constitutional amendments require greater public consultation and accountability than ordinary laws because the Constitution is the country's highest law.

Vuki also questions the limited time allocated for public submissions, pointing out that only three hours were provided for submissions in Suva.

She says the Commission decided not to make an oral presentation because it wanted ordinary members of the public to have more time to express their views.

Instead, the Commission submitted its views in writing before the deadline.

Vuki says the Commission also needed sufficient time to assess the proposed changes against the nine international human rights conventions she says Fiji has ratified.

She explains that this includes examining whether the proposed Bill of Rights meets Fiji's international human rights commitments.

Vuki says such an assessment requires careful consideration and cannot be completed without sufficient time.

She also points to the process that led to the 1997 Constitution, saying the committee responsible took about 13 months to complete its work.

Vuki believes Fiji should learn from previous constitutional review processes and allow enough time for meaningful public participation.

She stresses that Fijians must be given a fair opportunity to understand the proposed changes, ask questions and make informed submissions before decisions are made about the country's Constitution.

item.title: Voters free to choose who to vote for despite receiving free transport and food – FEO
item.description: Changes to electoral laws will allow political parties and candidates to arrange free transport to polling venues and provide meals and sheds for voters during the upcoming general elections. However, voters must make their own decisions on who they want to vote for.
item.content:encoded:
Changes to electoral laws will allow political parties and candidates to arrange free transport to polling venues and provide meals and sheds for voters during the upcoming general elections.

However, voters must make their own decisions on who they want to vote for.

This was highlighted by the Supervisor of Elections Ana Mataiciwa on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan, who says Fijians can expect to see sheds erected by political parties or independent candidates outside the 100-metres restricted area.

Mataiciwa stresses that at the end of the day, voters right to vote freely and in secret must be respected and they should not be pressured or forced to vote for any particular candidate because of the assistance they receive.

Insert: no one should force them 26th Oct

When questioned about measures to prevent political parties or candidates from pressuring voters, she says arrangements have been made with the Fiji Police Force and the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption.

She says presiding officers will also be in charge inside polling stations, while measures will also be in place to ensure compliance within the 100-metres restricted area.

The Supervisor is encouraging members of the public to report any incidents where voters are being pressured or forced to support a particular candidate.

She says complaints can be lodged through the Fijian Elections Office's complaints mechanism, while immediate concerns raised during polling hours can be addressed to prevent other voters from facing similar situations.

Mataiciwa adds that polling stations will open at 7.30am and close at 6pm.

She says formal complaints will be referred to the relevant authorities, including the Fiji Police Force and FICAC.

Mataiciwa says an Election Security Advisory Group has also been established to ensure complaints received before and during the elections are dealt with through the appropriate processes, which could include prosecution.

item.title: May 2000 coup showed how quickly people can lose their sense of safety - Kiran
item.description: The violence and fear that followed the May 2000 coup showed how quickly people can lose their sense of safety when law and order break down. Speaking during the Fiji Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearing, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran recalled how she learnt of the takeover on May 19th 2000, while working as a coordinator with the Fiji Council of Social Ser
item.content:encoded:
The violence and fear that followed the May 2000 coup showed how quickly people can lose their sense of safety when law and order break down.

Speaking during the Fiji Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearing, Minister for Women, Children and Social Protection, Sashi Kiran recalled how she learnt of the takeover on May 19th 2000, while working as a coordinator with the Fiji Council of Social Services.

Kiran says she had been attending a regular business meeting when she contacted the then Assistant Minister for National Affairs to ask about the situation, as a march and civil unrest were expected.

She says she was reassured that everything was under control and there was no immediate cause for concern.

However, Kiran says the situation changed rapidly when a message arrived on her mobile phone reporting that people had taken over Parliament.

She says an event planned for that day was cancelled, and staff were quickly organised to return home.

By the time they left, parts of the city had descended into looting and violence, leaving people experiencing fear, pressure and anguish.

Kiran says people began reaching out for help the following day, with women and children who had been abused among those needing support.

She says her focus at the time was on helping victims rather than identifying the perpetrators.

Kiran recalled how families were forced from their homes and sought shelter with relatives and other communities, while some people who offered shelter were also attacked.

She says she still remembered seeing people in tears, asking for help to remove their belongings from homes they feared they would be forced to leave.

Kiran says the experience raised serious questions about what could be done when people could no longer rely on the usual systems for protection.

Reflecting on the events, she says the crisis also highlighted the impact of political leaders’ words and the need to take public anger and concerns seriously before tensions escalate.

Kiran says there had been warnings and concerns about land issues before the violence, which deeply affected both communities.

She says leaders needed to pause, listen and engage in meaningful consultation when people expressed anger or raised concerns.

Kiran also stressed the importance of understanding iTaukei culture and sensitivities, saying the country needed greater engagement and dialogue.

She says democratic processes must be accompanied by genuine relationships with communities, including farmers and landowners, rather than one-sided engagement.

Kiran says the events of 2000 remained a lesson in the importance of listening to communities, recognising warning signs and ensuring people have systems they can turn to for protection.

item.title: Kadavu wants 2013 Constitution removed - Ratu Jona Bainivalu
item.description: Navitalai Naivalurua · 28/10/2026 Consultations on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill in Kadavu concluded today with the chiefs of the province making one submission on Kadavu's consolidated views on the proposed constitutional changes.
item.content:encoded:
Navitalai Naivalurua · 28/10/2026

Consultations on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill in Kadavu concluded today with the chiefs of the province making one submission on Kadavu's consolidated views on the proposed constitutional changes.

Turaga na Tui Naceva, Ratu Jona Bainivalu, informed the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill that Kadavu wants the removal of the 2013 Constitution.

Consultations will continue tomorrow at Levuka Town Hall on Ovalau at 10am.

The special committee is expected to finalise its report this weekend, ahead of the Constitution (Amendment) Bill's third and final reading in parliament on Monday.

item.title: El Niño risks highlight urgent need for investment in renewable energy – Gounder
item.description: Fijians could face electricity supply challenges during the El Niño crisis, as there have been calls for more investment in renewable energy, water infrastructure and roads should be prioritised to support the economy. This was highlighted by Permanent Secretary of Finance Shiri Gounder during a panel discussion on Fiji's economic outlook and reform priorities after World Bank Group Senior Economi
item.content:encoded:
Fijians could face electricity supply challenges during the El Niño crisis, as there have been calls for more investment in renewable energy, water infrastructure and roads should be prioritised to support the economy.

This was highlighted by Permanent Secretary of Finance Shiri Gounder during a panel discussion on Fiji's economic outlook and reform priorities after World Bank Group Senior Economist Tihomir Stucka questioned where the next additional dollar of productive public investment should go and what spending could be reduced or changed to make room for it over the medium-term.

Gounder says about 50 percent of Fiji's electricity is generated from hydropower and other renewable sources, and El Niño could create serious challenges for hydropower generation.

He says this could affect Energy Fiji Limited's operations and electricity supply, with wider impacts on the private sector.

Gounder says investment in renewable energy would help strengthen energy security and reduce Fiji's reliance on imported fuel.

He says the recent Middle East crisis highlighted concerns about fuel supply disruptions and their potential impact on the economy.

Gounder also identifies water supply and wastewater infrastructure as priorities, saying access to water has become a major challenge for the private sector.

He says investment in urban roads is also needed to address traffic congestion, which is affecting productivity.

Gounder says the Government needs to redirect funding from operating expenditure towards capital investment to address the country's infrastructure needs.

He says the public sector workforce, which has grown to more than 42,000 people, should be capped to prevent further increases.

Gounder says difficult decisions, greater public discussion and political consensus will be needed to make savings and direct funding towards productive investment.
